summary: Defines a certificate extension that links together a set of certificates belonging to the same end entity that can be treated as equivalent. Applications that keep state tied to a certificate can then recognize a renewed or reissued one. It is Experimental.

eli5.summary: If you replace your library card, the library should still know it is you. This extension lets a certificate point to other certificates for the same owner, so saved information is not lost.

questions: what is the other certificates extension
how to link equivalent x.509 certificates
how does certificate renewal linkage work
subtitle: An extension that lets linked certificates point back to each other so applications can recognize a renewed certificate.

tldr.problem: When a certificate expires and is renewed or when an entity changes certificate issuers, applications lose the connection between the old and new certificates, breaking application state like cached form data or password managers.
tldr.mechanism: The Other Certificates extension is a list of references to related certificates using the SCVPCertID structure. When a new certificate contains this extension, the CA asserts that the same entity holds the private keys for all linked certificates.
tldr.outcome: Applications can recognize that a new certificate belongs to the same entity as an old one, allowing them to preserve and transfer application-state information across certificate renewals without security risks.

today: RFC 5697 is Experimental. The extension provides a way for applications to recognize renewed or reissued certificates, though adoption depends on both CA and application support.

sections.title: Linking Certificates Across Renewals
sections.content:
Applications often store information linked to a certificate: a web browser might cache site logins or form data indexed by the server's certificate subject name, or a VPN client might store configuration tied to a gateway certificate. When a certificate expires and is renewed, or when an organization changes Certificate Authorities, the old certificate is no longer valid. Without a way to link the old and new certificates, applications lose the ability to find that stored state.

The Other Certificates extension solves this by allowing a CA to include in a new certificate a list of other certificates that the same entity holds private keys for. This linkage is not required to be simultaneous: an application can look at a new certificate, see that it references an old one, and use that link to find and reuse saved information.
sections.eli5: When you get a new certificate, it includes a note saying which old certificates belong to you, so the computer knows you are the same person.

sections.title: Extension Structure and Validation Rules
sections.content:
The extension is simply a sequence of references using the SCVPCertID structure from RFC 5055. Each reference includes a hash of the target certificate and the target's issuer name and serial number. The CA is asserting that the same end entity holds the private keys for all referenced certificates.

The extension MUST NOT be marked critical, meaning implementations that do not understand it can still process the certificate. CAs MUST only link certificates where the use case is clear: typically within a single application. For example, a CA SHOULD NOT link a web server certificate to a VPN gateway certificate unless those roles can be the same entity. CAs MUST validate that the end entity actually holds all the private keys for the linked certificates before issuing.
sections.eli5: The extension is a list pointing to other certificates. An app does not have to understand it to use the certificate, and the CA promises it has checked that you own all the linked keys.

sections.title: Application Use and Validation
sections.content:
When an application uses this extension, it MUST still validate all linked certificates according to RFC 5280, even if a parent CA is trusted. Each linked certificate must chain to a trust point and be valid in its own right. If any linked certificate has been revoked, the linkage MUST NOT be used.

The old and new certificates do not have to be valid at the same time. An application can cache information about a valid certificate and later, when presented with a new certificate that links back to the cached one, transfer the stored information to the new certificate. This is safe because the CA issuing the new certificate has asserted that the same entity controls both.
sections.eli5: When you use the linkage, you still check that both certificates are good and not revoked. You can trust information from the old certificate once the new one proves it came from the same entity.

sections.title: Security and Hash Function Strength
sections.content:
The SCVPCertID structure uses a hash to identify the target certificate. As hash function weaknesses emerge and collision attacks become practical, CAs and applications must ensure that the hash functions in use are currently acceptable. The default SHA-1 may not be considered strong enough; SHA-256 is preferred.

If the issuer of the new certificate is restricted by name constraints in a superior CA certificate, the new certificate can potentially link to an old certificate that would not be allowed under those constraints. Applications for which this is a risk SHOULD NOT use the extension.

In some contexts where the old certificate has expired and revocation information is no longer available, linking might be unsafe. Application developers SHOULD carefully consider whether to use this extension in such scenarios.
sections.eli5: Use a strong hash to identify the old certificate so someone cannot forge a fake one. Be careful if you link across authority boundaries, and check that old revocation information is still available if the old cert has expired.
